source.heading: PASSAGE I
source.directions: COMPREHENSION: Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows. The question carries 3 marks
source.attribution: Adapted from Peter Scott's article in Sunday Times.

passage.text: The African moralist has always regarded smoking as an indication of moral degradation.
A number of people have accepted the moralist idea on smoking while a good many people have remained indifferent to the moralist view and have continued to smoke.
The same argument has been applied to the consumption of alcohol.
The African moralist, basing his judgement on the behaviour of a few alcoholics, tend to regard the habit of taking alcohol as a sign of wretchedness.
The moralist holds the view that anybody who forms the habit of consuming alcohol will never do well in life.
While this may be true in respect of a few people in the society, the fear of the moralist has not been justified.

However, the economist is primarily interested in the habit of smoking and the consumption of alcohol in so far as they give satisfaction to smokers and drinkers and so generate supply of and demand for tobacco and alcohol.
Some moral principles associated with religion tend to lead on to economic problems.
Followers of certain religions are expected not to consume pork, take alcohol or smoke tobacco.
Devotees of some religious groups, on the other hand, can eat pork while others are expected to abstain from alcohol and smoking.

Strict observance of these moral rules could cripple the breweries, the cigarette factories and some businesses; however, there seems to be a growing number of alcohol consumers and cigarette smokers-a development which should be of interest to the economist.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the moralist idea is that

options.text: the smoking of cigarettes is bad and unacceptable
options.why: The moralist calls smoking a sign of moral degradation.

options.text: it is typically African not to smoke cigarettes
options.why: The passage describes a viewpoint. It does not call abstinence typical of all Africans.

options.text: people should accept a point of view only when they are convinced
options.why: The paragraph says people respond differently. It gives no rule about when to accept a view.

options.text: smoking is not good but a little alcohol may be permitted
options.why: The moralist also condemns the drinking habit and offers no exception for a small amount.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?

options.text: total abstinence from drinking and smoking is a religious obligation
options.why: The passage limits these rules to followers of certain religions.

options.text: smoking and drinking may have positive effects on the economy
options.why: From the economist's perspective, demand supports supply and related businesses.

options.text: every one ignores the moralist view on drinking and smoking
options.why: The passage says some people accepted the moralist's view.

options.text: people who drink or smoke surely die of cancer
options.why: The passage gives no claim about cancer.

questions.stem: The positions maintained by the moralist and the economist can be described as being

options.why: Both take specific positions, so neither is indifferent to the subject.
The moralist condemns the habits. The economist considers how they affect demand and supply.
The passage contrasts what the two people judge. It does not compare the strength of their feelings.
The moralist judges the habits morally. The economist considers their effect on supply and demand.
